1: the conductivity reading can be significantly inflated relative to a laboratory‑measured value — The supplied material states that errors can be large for low-pH waters but does not state that the error is an overestimation (inflated) or that it is relative to a laboratory-measured value.

4: their readings are very sensitive to air bubbles exposure to air and changes in the sample’s chemistry. — Searched the supplied material for any statement that ORP readings are sensitive to air bubbles exposure to air or changes in sample chemistry; found no such statement. The material mentions air bubbles only for conductivity and DO probes and mentions inconsistent ORP readings only when the liquid has very few electrons available for transfer.; When a bailer‑collected sample is tipped into a beaker bubbles can be introduced and the water can equilibrate with atmospheric gases producing the erratic values you are seeing. — Searched for a mechanism linking tipping a bailer sample into a beaker to bubble introduction and erratic ORP values; found no such statement. The material says subsamples are vulnerable to bias from changes in temperature pressure turbidity and gases but does not describe this specific mechanism or attribute erratic values to it.; ensuring the probe stays fully submerged and free of bubbles — Searched for any instruction that an ORP probe must be fully submerged and free of bubbles; found none. The material requires full submersion for the conductivity probe and warns about bubbles for conductivity and DO probes but gives no such requirement for ORP.; The probe itself is probably fine — Searched for any statement that the ORP probe is not faulty or is probably fine; found none. The material criticizes the sampling method but does not comment on the condition of the probe.

1: they can warm up (or cool down) before you read them on the bench — The supplied material states that temperature must be measured in situ and that subsamples must not be used but it does not state that grab samples can warm up or cool down before bench reading.

1: any bench (off‑site) reading — I searched the supplied material for any statement that the USGS requires documentation of bench or off-site readings and found no mention of 'bench' or 'off-site' in the retrieved documents; the cited quote only says 'Record field measurement and procedures on field forms' without specifying bench or off-site.

7: wait at least 2 minutes before you start recording the required series of readings — Searched the ORP excerpts (IORP_probe.pdf and USGS NFM A6.5) for a 2-minute stabilization wait; found no such requirement. The 2-minute wait appears only in the turbidity guidance (NFM A6.7).; five sequential measurements (for a flow‑through‑chamber) that are spaced at regular time intervals and are all within 10 percent of each other — Searched the ORP excerpts for a requirement of five sequential readings within 10 percent; found no such requirement. This criterion is from the turbidity guidance (NFM A6.7).; Instrument make and model (e.g. “Atlas Scientific Industrial ORP Probe part # ENV‑50‑ORP”) — Searched the ORP excerpts for a requirement to log instrument make and model; found none. The only mention of logging instrument make and model is in the turbidity guidance.; Date and time of the measurement — Searched the ORP excerpts for a requirement to log date; found only 'record the time' in NFM A6.5 not date.; Ambient pressure (if you are applying any barometric correction) – record the barometer reading to the nearest 1 mm Hg — Searched the ORP excerpts for barometric pressure logging; found none. The 1 mm Hg barometer reading is from DO calibration guidance.; Calibration status (date of last calibration any verification checks performed) — Searched the ORP excerpts for a requirement to log calibration status; found no specific mention of date of last calibration or verification checks. General log book requirement in NFM A6.0 mentions calibration history but not these specifics.; This ensures the data meet the USGS quality‑control requirements — Searched the ORP excerpts for a statement that logging these items ensures USGS quality-control requirements; found no such statement.

1: So the pod’s reading will rise by roughly 2 % per °C (or 0.5–3 % depending on water chemistry) unless the instrument’s built‑in temperature compensation has already adjusted the value to the 25 °C reference. — I searched the supplied material for any statement that this specific pod's conductivity reading changes by 2% per °C or that the pod has a temperature coefficient. The USGS excerpts describe general electrical conductivity behavior and specific conductance meter compensation factors and the probe spec sheet [1] does not mention a temperature coefficient or compensation for this pod. No excerpt applies these values to this pod's readings.

3: The temperature sensor should be accurate enough that its error contributes only a small fraction of the conductivity‑correction factor (≈ 2 % / °C). — Searched the retrieved documents for any statement of a conductivity temperature-compensation factor of about 2% per °C or any relationship between temperature sensor error and conductivity correction error; none was found. The only temperature-compensation discussion in the supplied material is in the previous assistant answer which is not grounding.; a temperature‑sensor error of ±0.2 °C will change the corrected conductivity by about ±0.4 % (0.2 °C × 2 %/°C) — Searched for any basis for the 2%/°C factor or the derived ±0.4% error; the supplied material contains no such figure or calculation. The cited excerpt 14 only gives temperature sensor accuracy specifications not conductivity correction effects.; a certified sensor with accuracy ≤±0.05 °C limits the conductivity‑correction error to about ±0.1 % — Searched for any statement linking certified sensor accuracy to a conductivity-correction error of ±0.1%; not found. The 2%/°C factor used in the calculation is unsupported by the supplied material.

2: Optional but recommended — I searched the supplied material for any statement that the zero-DO check is optional or recommended but the only reference is a required step in field-trip preparations: 'Perform a zero-DO sensor-performance check.' No source describes it as optional.; ensuring the sensor’s baseline is correct — I searched the supplied material for any statement that the zero-DO check ensures the sensor's baseline is correct and found no such reason or mechanism; the material only instructs to perform the check and specifies the acceptable reading threshold.

6: The USGS multiparameter‑instrument chapter (A6.8) gives field‑specific stability rules that are meant to be applied when you are using the sonde in the field and they are often tighter than the generic response‑time numbers that appear in the probe data sheets. — I searched the supplied material for any statement that A6.8 provides field-specific stability rules meant to be applied in the field and that they are often tighter than the probe data sheets. No such comparison or attribution is present.; Those figures describe how fast the sensor itself can settle under ideal lab conditions. — I searched the supplied material for any statement that the response times are under ideal lab conditions. No such characterization is present.; The USGS field manual adds a stability criterion for turbidity that requires three‑to‑five consecutive readings to be within 10 % of each other and to be monitored for 1–2 minutes or longer — I searched the supplied material for the quoted text 'Stability is reached if values for three (for in situ procedure) to five (for flowthrough‑chamber procedure) … are within 10 percent.' and 'Monitor turbidity readings for 1 to 2 minutes or longer to ensure that readings are stable'. These statements are not present in any retrieved document.; Similar 'allow the display to stabilize' language appears for all parameters in the multiparameter chapter — I searched the supplied material for any statement that such language applies to all parameters. The material only contains a general instruction to allow readings to stabilize within table 6.8–5 criteria but does not state it applies to all parameters.; Because the USGS guidance is the official field‑measurement protocol for the sonde you are deploying — I searched the supplied material for any statement that the USGS guidance is the official protocol for this specific sonde. No such attribution is present.; the stricter USGS stability rules take precedence for field work — I searched the supplied material for any statement that USGS stability rules are stricter and take precedence over manufacturer response times. No such precedence claim is present.

4: which makes the meter drift — The supplied material states that low-specific-conductance waters are challenging because the water is not sufficiently conductive and the liquid-junction potential is larger than normal but it does not state that this causes the meter to drift.; so the pH can be measured more reliably — The supplied material says KCl is recommended to minimize effects on the liquid junction potential but does not state that this makes pH measurement more reliable.; After the KCl amendment calibrate the pH probe with low‑ionic‑strength buffers (or the same KCl‑amended water) before taking the measurement. — The supplied material describes adding KCl to the sample and then measuring pH on an aliquot but does not instruct calibrating the probe with low-ionic-strength buffers or KCl-amended water.; Also be sure the probe is fully submerged free of air bubbles and that the calibration buffers match the sample’s ionic strength as recommended for low‑conductivity water — The supplied material does not contain advice to fully submerge the pH probe remove air bubbles or match calibration buffers to sample ionic strength for low-conductivity water.

3: at the temperature of measurement — Searched the A6.4 excerpt for a temperature qualifier on the recalibration condition; the excerpt says 'at the calibration temperature' for the check but the recalibration condition does not specify temperature.; before proceeding — Searched the A6.4 excerpt for a sequence requirement; the excerpt says 'recalibrate the pH electrode' without specifying 'before proceeding'.; ensures the electrode is still accurate after calibration — Searched the A6.4 excerpt for a statement of purpose; the excerpt only describes the check not its purpose.

1: The excerpts do not address whether the order of probes in a flow‑through cell matters. — The supplied material does address probe order in a flow-through cell e.g. [5] states 'install the pH sensor downstream from the conductivity sensor' and [12] states 'position the specific conductance probe upstream from the pH electrode.'

4: Waiting a few seconds (2‑3 s) after the wobble stops is usually enough to be confident the reading is stable. — I searched the supplied material for any guidance on waiting a specific number of seconds after the display stops wobbling and found no such recommendation. The response times (90% in 1s 95% in 1s) are given but no advice on how long to wait after stabilization.; After the numbers stop wobbling watch the display for a few seconds (conductivity ORP pH). — I searched for any instruction to watch the display for a few seconds after the numbers stop wobbling and found no such guidance in the supplied material.; Field practice is to wait until the reading stops drifting often 5–10 minutes — I searched for a statement that field practice is to wait 5-10 minutes for DO readings to stabilize. The only 5-10 minute stabilization time in the supplied material is for the zero-DO solution check (source [5]) not for general DO measurement.; For DO stay until the value no longer drifts for at least a minute and ideally 5‑10 minutes if the water temperature may be changing. — I searched for any duration of 'at least a minute' for DO stabilization and found none. The 5-10 minute figure is from the zero-DO solution check not for general measurement and the condition about water temperature changing is not mentioned in the supplied material.

5: in a calibrated water bath — The supplied material describes a 'refrigerated water bath' and 'water bath' but never calls the bath 'calibrated'.; also recommended before each field deployment — The material requires verification at least once every 12 months but does not recommend it before each field deployment.; or whenever the sensor has been out of service for a long period — No excerpt mentions verifying the temperature sensor after a long out-of-service period.; or whenever you suspect drift — No excerpt mentions verifying the temperature sensor when drift is suspected.; a calibrated thermometer — The material refers to a 'certified or traceable sensor' or a 'certified reference thermometer' not a 'calibrated thermometer'.

5: at a typical atmospheric pressure (≈ 760 mm Hg) — The supplied material provides solubility values at various pressures but never states that 760 mm Hg is typical; no excerpt characterizes any pressure as typical.; At 15 °C the maximum dissolved-oxygen concentration is 9.27 mg L⁻¹ — The supplied tables give 9.27 mg/L for 15.0 °C only at 700 mm Hg; at 760 mm Hg the value is 10.08 mg/L so the claim as stated (with the 760 mm Hg context) is not supported.; At 20 °C the maximum dissolved-oxygen concentration is 8.36 mg L⁻¹ — The supplied tables give 8.36 mg/L for 20.0 °C only at 700 mm Hg; at 760 mm Hg the value is 9.09 mg/L so the claim as stated is not supported.; The temperature rise from 15 °C to 20 °C therefore reduces the saturation level by about 0.91 mg L⁻¹ (9.27 – 8.36) — This arithmetic relies on the unsupported 9.27 and 8.36 values; the supported values at 760 mm Hg would yield a different difference.; Subtracting the temperature-driven change leaves an additional ≈ 0.5 mg L⁻¹ decrease — This is derived from the unsupported 0.91 mg/L reduction so the resulting 0.5 mg/L figure is not grounded in the supplied material.

2: so a 0.5 °C error will affect the DO value — The supplied material states that temperature must be known to determine the theoretical amount of oxygen but does not state that a 0.5°C error will affect the DO value.; a half‑degree offset will also shift the reported pH — The supplied material states that pH meters automatically compensate for temperature differences but does not state that a half-degree offset will shift the reported pH.

1: deploy at least four evenly spaced points (or more depending on how heterogeneous the flow is) using an EWI or EDI layout — I searched the supplied material for a statement that a minimum of four evenly spaced measurement points is required for both EWI and EDI methods. The EDI section says 'Divide the stream into a minimum of four increments' but does not say they are evenly spaced and the EWI section says 'a minimum of 10 equal-width increments is recommended' for streams 5 ft or greater and for smaller streams 'use as many increments as is practical but they must be equally spaced and a minimum of 3 inches apart.' No source states a minimum of four evenly spaced points for either method.

5: the same calculation steps (look up the factor for the measured temperature and specific conductance then multiply the raw DO value by that factor) are used for any pod regardless of location — The supplied material does not state that the salinity-correction procedure applies to all pods regardless of location; it only provides the table and its description.; the specific conductance will be much lower than 50 000 µS cm⁻¹ — The supplied material does not provide any specific conductance values for fresh water or state that fresh water has conductance much lower than 50 000 µS/cm.; the factor you retrieve from the table will be close to 1.0 — The supplied table only lists factors for specific conductance values from 45 000 to 59 000 µS/cm; it does not give factors for lower conductance or state that they approach 1.0.; the salinity correction will be minimal — The supplied material does not state that the correction is minimal for fresh water or for low specific conductance.; you still apply the procedure to obtain the properly compensated DO value — The supplied material does not state that the procedure should be applied to all pods or that it is necessary for fresh water; it only describes the table and its use.

1: the variability among consecutive measurements falls within the limits shown in table 6.0‑1 — The supplied material references 'stabilization criteria in table 6.0–1' but does not state that these criteria concern variability among consecutive measurements or provide the limits.

1: The SOP calls for an air-calibration (Procedure 1) rather than a solution calibration. — I searched the supplied material for a statement that the SOP requires air calibration over solution calibration. The documents describe both Procedure 1 (air) and Procedure 2 (air-saturated water) and recommend the wet-towel method for field sites but none state that air calibration is required instead of solution calibration.

5: gently inverting or shaking the bottle — The supplied material only instructs to resuspend calibrants by 'inverting the calibrant 25 times' (excerpt 28) and does not mention shaking or the qualifier 'gently'.; If the settled layer can be fully re‑suspended and the solution looks homogeneous you may proceed — The material does not state that a resuspended homogeneous calibrant may be used; it only says to resuspend calibrants and warns against flocculated suspensions.; you must note the potential for bias — The material requires noting bias for turbidity samples when particle settling occurs but not for calibrants.; the risk of degradation or flocculation is high — The material does not discuss degradation or flocculation risk from long storage; it only states that calibrants must not exceed shelf life and that some stock solutions are stable only for about one day.; the safest practice is to discard the old calibrant and prepare a fresh one — The material does not recommend discarding old calibrants; it only says to not use expired calibrants and to prepare fresh calibrants as needed.

4: you must contact the instrument manufacturer — I searched the supplied material for any statement that contacting the manufacturer is mandatory but the excerpt only says 'contact the instrument manufacturer' without the word 'must'.; because the sensor may need repair or replacement of the luminophore module — I searched for any statement that the sensor may need repair or replacement but the excerpt only says 'inquire whether the luminophore module should be replaced' and does not mention repair or a 'may need' reason.; confirms the zero-DO calibration succeeded — I searched for any statement that a reading within ±0.2 mg/L confirms calibration success but the excerpt describes a performance check not a calibration and does not say it confirms success.; a higher reading indicates a problem with the sensor that requires further troubleshooting or service — I searched for any statement that a higher reading indicates a problem or requires troubleshooting or service but the excerpt only instructs to contact the manufacturer and does not characterize the reading as indicating a problem or requiring troubleshooting/service.

1: The USGS A6.2 table 6.2‑2 does not include the 35 °C solubility value in the provided excerpts. — The supplied material includes a table with a row for 35.0 °C (e.g. in excerpt [7] showing solubility values at 35.0 °C across pressures) so the claim that it is not included is unsupported.

2: The specific freshwater equilibrium dissolved‑oxygen saturation value at 20 °C and 760 mm Hg is not present in the provided excerpts. — The supplied excerpts include table 6.2–2 with a value for 20.0 °C at 760 mmHg (9.09 mg/L) in excerpt [10] so the claim of absence is unsupported.; from the example in the document【14】 — The 8.97 mg/L value at 20 °C and 750 mmHg appears in excerpt [24] (the example salinity correction) not in excerpt [14]; the attribution to document [14] is unsupported.

1: so that the standard falls within the ±3 % tolerance required for measurements above 100 µS/cm — I searched the supplied material for any statement that a calibration standard must fall within ±3% of the expected value or that the ±3% tolerance applies to the calibration standard itself. The documents only apply the ±3% tolerance to check standards (e.g. 'Measurements of specific conductance standards that are within ±5 μS/cm of the certified values for measurements ≤100 μS/cm or ±3 percent of the certified values for measurements >100 μS/cm are considered accurate') not to the selection of the calibration standard.

4: A reading of 6 µS/cm in your de-ionized water shows that the water still contains a small amount of dissolved ions. — The supplied material describes the operating principle of conductivity probes but does not state that a specific low reading indicates the presence of dissolved ions nor does it provide any interpretation of a 6 µS/cm reading.; In practice such a low value is typical for de-ionized water — The supplied material does not state any typical conductivity value for de-ionized water.; and does not by itself indicate a fault with the probe — The supplied material does not discuss whether a low conductivity reading indicates a probe fault.; though it does confirm that the water is not completely ion-free — The supplied material does not state that a non-zero conductivity reading confirms the presence of ions or that the water is not ion-free.

2: differ by no more than 10 % of each other — The supplied material states stability is reached when sequential readings are 'within 10 percent' but does not define that as a difference between readings; I searched for any specification that the 10 percent refers to pairwise differences and found none.; the sensor has stopped “creeping” — The supplied material describes stability in terms of readings being within 10 percent but never states that this condition means the sensor has stopped creeping; I searched for any mention of 'creeping' or a causal link between stability and sensor behavior and found none.

3: For a yearly calibration verification you need at least five verification points spread across the temperature range you expect to measure plus two additional points that are taken no more than six months from the five-point set — The supplied material states 'The minimum number of verification points is two' (in [5]) and does not state that five points are required for yearly verification; the five-point requirement appears only for establishing a traceable sensor not for the annual calibration verification of a deployed sensor.; a suitable five-point set could be: 4 °C 6 °C 8 °C 10 °C 12 °C — The supplied material does not support a five-point set for yearly verification; the minimum is two points and the answer's proposed set of five points is not grounded in any excerpt.; The two extra checks taken within six months of the main set can be any temperatures within that range for example 5 °C and 11 °C. — The supplied material does not support that two extra checks are part of the yearly verification; the two-point check within six months is part of the traceable sensor requirement not the annual calibration verification of a deployed sensor.

1: an ORP reading expressed in mV is an Eh value — The supplied material defines Eh as a measure of oxidation-reduction potential and describes Eh measurements using a platinum electrode but nowhere does it state that an ORP probe reading in millivolts is the same as an Eh value. The documents treat ORP sensors and Eh equipment as distinct (e.g. [6] mentions an ORP sensor connected to a multiparameter instrument and separately requires Eh equipment to be tested) so the equivalence claim is not grounded.

3: If the reading is within either the ±5 mV manufacturer spec or the +10 mV EPA limit the probe is considered to have passed. — I searched the supplied material for a statement that meeting either the ±5 mV accuracy spec or the +10 mV EPA post-calibration check constitutes passing. The material gives ±5 mV as ORP accuracy (in [7]) and +10 mV as an EPA post-calibration criterion (in [32]) but nowhere does it say that being within either of these means the probe has passed.; Look for drift: repeat the measurement after a short interval; the value should not change by more than a few millivolts — I searched the supplied material for a specific drift tolerance or a statement that the value should not change by more than a few millivolts. The material only says 'If they change re-calibrate' (in [6]) and does not provide any numeric drift limit or instruction to repeat after a short interval.; If the probe meets these steps—reading the ZoBell’s solution within the ±5 mV (or +10 mV) window with stable battery voltage and a clean reference electrode—it is considered calibrated and ready for deployment. — I searched the supplied material for a statement that meeting these conditions (reading within ±5 mV or +10 mV stable battery voltage clean reference electrode) means the probe is considered calibrated and ready for deployment. The material describes procedures and checks but does not define a pass/fail criterion that combines these elements or state that meeting them constitutes calibration readiness.

3: dissolved‑oxygen probes often require 5–10 min — The supplied material only mentions a 5–10 minute stabilization wait in the context of the zero-DO solution check (e.g. 【8†"wait for reading to stabilize (usually within 5–10 minutes)"】) not as a general statement about dissolved-oxygen probes requiring that time to reach a steady signal.; the USGS chapters do not list a separate “settle‑down” waiting period for Eh/ORP — I searched the supplied USGS excerpts for any statement about ORP/Eh stabilization or a settle-down waiting period and found none; the material does not address whether such a period is listed or omitted.; the lack of a settle‑time note reflects the probe’s fast response not an omission of the parameter — No supplied excerpt provides a reason for the absence of a settle-time note for ORP/Eh; this causal explanation is not grounded in the retrieved documents.

1: The request needs guidance on how to handle a required step that cannot be performed which is not covered in the provided excerpts. — I searched the supplied material for any guidance on departing from or modifying a required step when it cannot be performed and found that the excerpts do address this: e.g. [14] states 'Departure from or modifications to stipulated requirements if necessary for accomplishing specific data-quality requirements or study objectives must be independently quality assured and documented' (also in [23] and [28]). Therefore the claim that this is 'not covered in the provided excerpts' is unsupported.
